newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: FEATURE - Inflation nags in pre-election Irish budget.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Inflation nags in pre-election Irish budget.

text.p: Germany struggles. Britain dithers. But tiny Ireland sits the final examinations for membership of EMU this month knowing that its only problem is success.

Finance Minister Ruairi Quinn unveils his last full budget on January 22 in what he has called a crucial test of Dublin's ability to meet the Maastricht criteria which would allow one of the EU's smallest states to take part in its biggest project.

Membership of Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) is the declared goal of successive Irish governments and the January budget, together with a mini-budget later this year, will be Dublin's last chance to prove its credentials for a 1999 start.

Quinn's counterparts in Bonn, Paris and Rome would envy the data he will use to illustrate how prudent financial management has earned Ireland the title of "model European state" a tag conferred by EU Commission President Jacques Santer last month.
IRELAND'S LITTLE ECONOMIC MIRACLE

The country's debt has fallen for the first time in 39 years. Government borrowing as a percentage of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is one percent compared to the three percent ceiling imposed by Maastricht.
The economy is set to expand by five percent this year after six percent in 1996 -- much of the rest of Europe is struggling to maintain growth of around two percent.

Helped by EU modernisation grants and an aggressive campaign to lure foreign hi-tech investment, the Irish economy has not contracted in the past 10 years and never even caught a cold when the rest of Europe went down with recessionary pneumonia.
Unemployment, the country's perennial black spot, has eased with the creation of an unprecedented 50,000 jobs to trim the total out of work to less than 11 percent of the workforce.
TAX CUT CLAMOUR FUELS INFLATION WORRIES

Quinn's main problem will be that voters are expecting tax cuts to reward the 3.5 million population for a decade of economic expansion and the boasts of successive governments that Ireland is Europe's little economic miracle.

Such expectations, together with an unexpected surge in private sector credit growth, have raised fears within government and financial circles of an inflationary surge that would spoil Ireland's EMU party.

Under Maastricht guidelines, inflation must not exceed that of the three best-performing EU states by more than 1.5 percent and all the signs are that Irish inflation is on the increase after a benign 1.6 percent in 1996.

"There is no doubt that inflation is going to be higher in 1997 than in 1996," said stockbrokers Bloxham in a research note. It predicted that inflation will skirt 2.5 percent, dangerously close to the Maastricht limits.

Voter expectations have been fuelled by the release in the past three weeks of data showing that public finances are in the best shape for 20 years and by the fact that 1997 is an election year -- a poll must be held by November.
EARLY ELECTION SEEN TO CASH IN ON BUDGET

Quinn, an erudite man who is as skilled at fending off parliamentary sniping as he is at handling complex financial data, has denied that there will be any link between the budget and an election many expect by May at the latest.

But even members of Prime Minister John Bruton's ruling coalition of Fine Gael, the Labour Party and Democratic Left, acknowledge that it would be foolhardy to peddle austerity months before testing popularity at the ballot box.

Generous tax cuts -- a media bandwagon is predicting a reduction in the basic rate from 27 percent to 26 percent -- to both income and payroll tax have raised worries of a consumer spending boom that would distort tidy inflation data.
"No Irish finance minister would go into an election year by hitting voters on the head," said one senior member of Bruton's left-right coalition.
CENTRAL BANK REPORTED WORRIED BY CREDIT GROWTH

Inflation concerns have been increased by central bank data showing that the annualised rate of private sector credit growth rose to 16.4 percent last November from a revised 14.4 percent the previous month.
"There is very little for the central bank to smile about in these latest banking figures," said Bloxham, which is predicting an interest rate rise in the first quarter of this year.
"The central bank must implement interest/exchange rate policies that will enable Ireland to qualify for EMU and if that means higher interest rates in the short term, so be it."
The opposition, led by the Fianna Fail party of Bertie Ahern, is already accusing Bruton's coalition of squandering the fruits of growth with runaway public spending.

Quinn acknowledged last month that 1997 government spending would be 13.01 billion Irish pounds or punts ($21.64 billion), an increase of 6.1 percent in nominal terms or 3.9 percent in real terms. This will have to be increased even further to take account of a generous public sector pay deal.
A POPULAR OR EFFECTIVE 1997 BUDGET?
This was after repeated pledges to limit any increase in government spending to an average annual rate of two percent in real terms.

In the event the additional spending was more than covered when Quinn's ministry unveiled data last week showing that 1996 exchequer borrowing was 437 million pounds, undershooting the government target of 729 million.
The equation was tilted towards the government's side by a 10.5 percent rise in tax revenue against a 6.5 percent target.

But opposition finance spokesman Charlie McCreevy rushed to attack by showing that government spending was now out of control and the nation's wealth was being "thrown away" on the very eve of Irish membership of Europe's exclusive EMU club. ($1=.6013 Punt)
